title: Rout a curved edge on a router table: brace the board on the starting pin and pivot it onto the bearing before feeding
instruction: Rout the rabbet along the board's curved edge on the router table, then leave the board on the table past the bit.
context: Cabinetmakers and woodworking machine operators (O*NET 51-7011.00, 51-7042.00) rout rabbets and profiles on curved parts with a bearing-guided bit on a router table, where no fence can steady the work. Router-table manuals all give the same start: brace the board against the starting pin, a steel pin in the insert plate beside the bit, and pivot it about the pin into the spinning bit until its edge rides the bit's bearing; only then swing it off the pin and feed it right to left round the bearing, against the bit's rotation, until it is clear of the bit, keeping hands at least 3 inches from the bit. The pin takes the cutter's first bite, and a curved board pushed straight into the bit has nothing to resist that bite, so the bit grabs the board and throws it or pulls the hands toward the cutter. Unlike #1218 (where to press a held part on a buffing wheel), the board here is pivoted in from a fixed pin, then fed along a curve against the cutter's rotation.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. The table is the router table's top, a light gray laminate (x 9 to 49, y -27 to 35). A black phenolic insert plate, 23.5 x 30 cm (9.25 x 11.75 in), lies flush in it centered on the bit (x 21.3 to 44.8, y -9 to 21). The bit is a 3/8 in rabbeting bit with its axis at x 33, y 6: a red-coated cutter 3.18 cm across (1.25 in) standing 6.4 mm above the table, and on its tip a 1.27 cm (0.5 in) steel ball bearing from 6.6 to 11.4 mm above the table, held by a screw. Seen from above the bit turns counterclockwise (the router hangs upside down under the table), so its front cutting edge moves to the robot's right and work is fed right to left. The starting pin, a steel pin 6.4 mm (0.25 in) across and 3 cm tall, stands in the insert plate at x 33.75, y 1, 5 cm to the bit's right. The work is a cherry board, 25 x 15 cm and 1.27 cm (0.5 in) thick, 220 g, with one long side band-sawn to a 30 cm radius (2.7 cm of bow, a 25.8 cm curve). It lies flat on the table to the right of the bit with its curve toward the bit, turned 14 degrees counterclockwise from square: the curve runs from (33.5, -18.1) at its right (trailing) end to (27.4, 6.2) at its left (leading) end, and the back corners are at (21.6, -21.0) and (15.5, 3.2). It is 2.4 cm from the pin and 4.4 cm from the bit's axis. It slides and turns flat on the table. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. The board is braced while any part of it is within 1.5 mm of the pin's surface and its curve is not yet on the bearing; while braced it can only turn about the pin. The cutter is the bit's 15.9 mm radius; the curve rides the bearing while the bit's axis is within the bearing's radius plus 1.5 mm of it. Score 0, irreversibly, if the board ever meets the cutter other than by being turned into it about the pin while braced (braced at that step and the one before): fed into the bit off the pin, shoved onto pin and bit in one step, or pushed back into the bit after once leaving it (a grab). Score 0, irreversibly, if a tool point comes within 7.6 cm (3 in, the router-table rule for hands) of the bit's axis with the pad tips within 5 cm of the table. Nothing counts while a hand is still on the board: pad tips over it (grown 1 cm) within 1.5 cm above its top score 0. Routed length is the stretch of the curve, counted in 2 mm pieces, that the bearing passed over in a cut begun on the pin, fed right to left (the contact moving toward the trailing end); feeding the other way, a climb cut, routes nothing. Otherwise, at the end: 1.0 with at least 18 cm routed (70% of the 25.8 cm curve: a start braced on this pin enters the curve 3 to 7 cm in from its leading end, a stretch done in a second pass), the board 5 mm clear of the cutter with its trailing end past the bit's axis, both arms back home (each tool point within 3 cm of its start) and still for 1 s; 0.9 the same with the arms elsewhere; 0.75 with 18 cm routed but the board left on or before the bit; 0.5 with at least 9 cm routed (half); 0.25 with the curve brought onto the bearing from the pin but not fed round; 0 otherwise, including doing nothing. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial the router is unplugged and the bit is a dummy (a 0.5 in bearing on a bolt, the cutter's circle painted on the plate), since a still bit's carbide would stop the board short of the bearing. Film from above with the board's edge pencil-marked every centimeter: check the board touched the pin before it crossed the cutter circle and stayed on it until the edge met the bearing, read off the marks that passed the bearing, and check where the board ended.
reset_notes: Lay the board back flat on the table to the right of the bit at its start pose (corners as in the setup), curve toward the bit, 2 cm off the pin. In a real trial the dummy bit cuts nothing, so the same board serves every trial.
fidelity: The bit is modeled and does not cut or spin: a cut is the board's outline inside the cutter's radius, and the routed stretch is drawn as a pale band on the board's top (the real rabbet is underneath). The board slides flat on joints with drag as damping and turns stiffer than a real one when off the pin; while braced on the pin it can only turn about it. The bearing (frictionless, as it rolls) and the pin are real colliders, and the bit guard is left off for the cameras.
